entries.fba4270a1d909a42870e178e8aa62c88c6b90b2b: <div sID="gen33723" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1John.4" sID="1John.4"/> <div eID="gen33723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33724" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33725" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the apostle exhorts to try spirits (<reference osisRef="1John.4.1">ver. 1</reference>), gives a note to try by (<reference osisRef="1John.4.2-1John.4.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>), shows who are of the world and who of God (<reference osisRef="1John.4.4-1John.4.6">ver. 4-6</reference>), urges Christian love by divers considerations (<reference osisRef="1John.4.7-1John.4.16">ver. 7-16</reference>), describes our love to God, and the effect of it, <reference osisRef="1John.4.17-1John.4.21">ver. 17-21</reference>.
entries.b9c56f59181b7fae28157e2d6f88f626020c56f3: <div eID="gen33725" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33724" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Concerning Antichrist. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33726" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God: <hi type="super">3</hi> And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is that <hi type="italic">spirit</hi> of antichrist, whereof ye have heard that it should come; and even now already is it in the world. <div eID="gen33726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33727" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having said that God's dwelling in and with us may be known by <hi type="italic">the Spirit that he hath given us,</hi> intimates that that Spirit may be discerned and distinguished from other spirits that appear in the world; and so here, <div eID="gen33727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33728" type="x-p"/> I. He calls the disciples, to whom he writes, to caution and scrutiny about the spirits and spiritual professors that had now risen. 1. To caution: "<hi type="italic">Beloved, believe not every spirit;</hi> regard not, trust not, follow not, every pretender to the Spirit of God, or every professor of vision, or inspiration, or revelation from God." Truth is the foundation of simulation and counterfeits; there had been real communications from the divine Spirit, and therefore others pretended thereto. God will take the way of his own wisdom and goodness, though it may be liable to abuse; he has sent inspired teachers to the world, and given us a supernatural revelation, though others may be so evil and so impudent as to pretend the same; every pretender to the divine Spirit, or to inspiration, and extraordinary illumination thereby, is not to be believed. Time was when the spiritual man (the man of the Spirit, who made a great noise about, and boast of, the Spirit) was mad, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.7">Hos. ix. 7</reference>. 2. To scrutiny, to examination of the claims that are laid to the Spirit: <hi type="italic">But try the spirits, whether they be of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">v. 1</reference>. God has given of his Spirit in these latter ages of the world, but not to all who profess to come furnished therewith; to the disciples is allowed a judgment of discretion, in reference to the spirits that would be believed and trusted in the affairs of religion. A reason is given for this trial: <hi type="italic">Because many false prophets have gone out into the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">v. 1</reference>. There being much about the time of our Saviour's appearance in the world a general expectation among the Jews of a Redeemer to Israel, and the humiliation, spiritual reformation, and sufferings of the Saviour being taken as a prejudice against him, others were induced to set up as prophets and messiahs to Israel, according to the Saviour's prediction, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.23-Matt.24.24">Matt. xxiv. 23, 24</reference>. It should not seem strange to us that false teachers set themselves up in the church: it was so in the apostles' times; fatal is the spirit of delusion, sad that men should vaunt themselves for prophets and inspired preachers that are by no means so! <div eID="gen33728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33729" type="x-p"/> II. He gives a test whereby the disciples may try these pretending spirits. These spirits set up for prophets, doctors, or dictators in religion, and so they were to be tried by their doctrine; and the test whereby in that day, or in that part of the world where the apostle now resided (for in various seasons, and in various churches, tests were different), must be this: <hi type="italic">Hereby know you the Spirit of God, Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh</hi> (or <hi type="italic">that confesseth Jesus Christ that came in the flesh), is of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.2">v. 2</reference>. Jesus Christ is to be confessed as the Son of God, the eternal life and Word, that was with the Father from the beginning; as the Son of God that came into, and came in, our human mortal nature, and therein suffered and died at Jerusalem. He who confesses and preaches this, by a mind supernaturally instructed and enlightened therein, does it by the Spirit of God, or God is the author of that illumination. On the contrary, "<hi type="italic">Every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ that came in the flesh) is not of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.3">v. 3</reference>. God has given so much testimony to Jesus Christ, who was lately here in the world, and in <hi type="italic">the flesh</hi> (or in a fleshly body like ours), though now in heaven, that you may be assured that any impulse or pretended inspiration that contradicts this is far from being from heaven and of God." The sum of revealed religion is comprehended in the doctrine concerning Christ, his person and office. We see then the aggravation of a systematic opposition to him and it. <hi type="italic">And this is that spirit of antichrist whereof you have heard that it should come, and even now already is it in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.3">v. 3</reference>. It was foreknown by God that antichrists would arise, and antichristian spirits oppose his Spirit and his truth; it was foreknown also that one eminent antichrist would arise, and make a long and fatal war against the Christ of God, and his institution, and honour, and kingdom in the world. This great antichrist would have his way prepared, and his rise facilitated, by other less antichrists, and the spirit of error working and disposing men's minds for him: the antichristian spirit began betimes, even in the apostles' days. Dreadful and unsearchable is the judgment of God, that persons should be given over to an antichristian spirit, and to such darkness and delusion as to set themselves against the Son of God and all the testimony that the Father hath given to the Son! But we have been forewarned that such opposition would arise; we should therefore cease to be offended, and the more we see the word of Christ fulfilled the more confirmed we should be in the truth of it.
entries.bff50e0cefe9d77aad2efd74e1ce7126625eff88: <div eID="gen33729" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Danger of Antichristian Spirit. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33730" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Ye are of God, little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world. <hi type="super">5</hi> They are of the world: therefore speak they of the world, and the world heareth them. <hi type="super">6</hi> We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error. <div eID="gen33730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33731" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle encourages the disciples against the fear and danger of this seducing antichristian spirit, and that by such methods as these:—1. He assures them of a more divine principle in them: "<hi type="italic">You are of God, little children,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">You are God's little children. We are of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.6">v. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">We are born of God,</hi> taught of God, anointed of God, and so secured against infectious fatal delusions. God has his chosen, who shall not be mortally seduced." 2. He gives them hope of victory: "<hi type="italic">And have overcome them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.4">v. 4</reference>. You have hitherto overcome these deceivers and their temptations, and there is good ground of hope that you will do so still, and that upon these two accounts:"—(1.) "There is a strong preserver within you: <hi type="italic">Because greater is he that is in you than he that is in the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.4">v. 4</reference>. The Spirit of God dwells in you, and that Spirit is more mighty than men of devils." It is a great happiness to be under the influence of the Holy Ghost. (2.) "You are not of the same temper with these deceivers. The Spirit of God hath framed your mind for God and heaven; <hi type="italic">but they are of the world.</hi> The spirit that prevails in them leads them to this world; their heart is addicted thereto; they study the pomp, the pleasure, and interest of the world: <hi type="italic">and therefore speak they of the world;</hi> they profess a worldly messiah and saviour; they project a worldly kingdom and dominion; the possessions and treasures of the world would they engross to themselves, forgetting that the true Redeemer's <hi type="italic">kingdom is not of this world.</hi> This worldly design procures them proselytes: <hi type="italic">The world heareth them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.5">v. 5</reference>. They are followed by such as themselves: the world will love its own, and its own will love it. But those are in a fair way to conquer pernicious seductions who have conquered the love of this seducing world." Then, 3. He represents to them that though their company might be the smaller, yet it was the better; they had more divine and holy knowledge: "<hi type="italic">He that knoweth God heareth us.</hi> He who knows the purity and holiness of God, the love and grace of God, the truth and faithfulness of God, the ancient word and prophecies of God, the signals and testimonials of God, must know that he is with us; and he who knows this will attend to us, and abide with us." He that is well furnished with natural religion will the more faithfully cleave to Christianity. <hi type="italic">He that knoweth God</hi> (in his natural and moral excellences, revelations, and works) <hi type="italic">heareth us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.6">v. 6</reference>. As, on the contrary, "<hi type="italic">He that is not of God heareth not us.</hi> He who knows not God regards not us. He that is not <hi type="italic">born of God</hi> (walking according to his natural disposition) walks not with us. The further any are from God (as appears in all ages) the further they are from Christ and his faithful servants; and the more addicted persons are to this world the more remote they are from the spirit of Christianity. Thus you have a distinction between us and others: <hi type="italic">Hereby know we the Spirit of truth and the spirit of error,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.6">v. 6</reference>. This doctrine concerning the Saviour's person leading you from the world to God is a signature of <hi type="italic">the Spirit of truth,</hi> in opposition to <hi type="italic">the spirit of error.</hi> The more pure and holy any doctrine is the more likely is it to be of God."
entries.1e2378349f21a3b85b2ed9a77e0a339b2d8c200c: <div eID="gen33731" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Brotherly Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33732" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. 8 He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. 9 In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. <hi type="super">10</hi> Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son <hi type="italic">to be</hi> the propitiation for our sins. <hi type="super">11</hi> Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another. <hi type="super">12</hi> No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us. <hi type="super">13</hi> Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit. <div eID="gen33732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33733" type="x-p"/> As <hi type="italic">the Spirit of truth</hi> is known by doctrine (thus spirits are to be tried), it is known by love likewise; and so here follows a strong fervent exhortation to holy Christian love: <hi type="italic">Beloved, let us love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.7">v. 7</reference>. The apostle would unite them in his love, that he might unite them in love to each other: "<hi type="italic">Beloved,</hi> I beseech you, by the love I bear to you, that you put on unfeigned mutual love." This exhortation is pressed and urged with variety of argument: as, <div eID="gen33733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33734" type="x-p"/> I. From the high and heavenly descent of love: <hi type="italic">For love is of God.</hi> He is the fountain, author, parent, and commander of love; it is the sum of his law and gospel: <hi type="italic">And every one that loveth</hi> (whose spirit is framed to judicious holy love) <hi type="italic">is born of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.7">v. 7</reference>. The Spirit of God is the Spirit of love. The new nature in the children of God is the offspring of his love: and the temper and complexion of it is love. <hi type="italic">The fruit of the Spirit is love,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Gal. v. 22</reference>. Love comes down from heaven. <div eID="gen33734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33735" type="x-p"/> II. Love argues a true and just apprehension of the divine nature: <hi type="italic">He that loveth knoweth God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.7">v. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">He that loveth not knoweth not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.8">v. 8</reference>. What attribute of the divine Majesty so clearly shines in all the world as his communicative goodness, which is love. The wisdom, the greatness, the harmony, and usefulness of the vast creation, which so fully demonstrate his being, do at the same time show and prove his love; and natural reason, inferring and collecting the nature and excellence of the most absolute perfect being, must collect and find that he is most highly good: and <hi type="italic">he that loveth not</hi> (is not quickened by the knowledge he hath of God to the affection and practice of love) <hi type="italic">knoweth not God;</hi> it is a convictive evidence that the sound and due knowledge of God dwells not in such a soul; his love must needs shine among his primary brightest perfections; <hi type="italic">for God is love</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">v. 8</reference>), his nature and essence are love, his will and works are primarily love. Not that this is the only conception we ought to have of him; we have found that he <hi type="italic">is light as well as love</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>), and God is principally love to himself, and he has such perfections as arise from the necessary love he must bear to his necessary existence, excellence, and glory; but love is natural and essential to the divine Majesty: <hi type="italic">God is love.</hi> This is argued from the display and demonstration that he hath given of it; as, 1. That he hath loved us, such as we are: <hi type="italic">In this was manifest the love of God towards us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.9">v. 9</reference>), towards us mortals, us ungrateful rebels. <hi type="italic">God commandeth his love towards us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">Rom. v. 8</reference>. Strange that God should love impure, vain, vile, dust and ashes! 2. That he has loved us at such a rate, at such an incomparable value as he has given for us; he has given his own, only-beloved, blessed Son for us: <hi type="italic">Because that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.9">v. 9</reference>. This person is in some peculiar distinguishing way the Son of God; he is the only-begotten. Should we suppose him begotten as a creature or created being, he is not the only-begotten. Should we suppose him a natural necessary eradication from the Father's glory or glorious essence, or substance, he must be the only-begotten: and then it will be a mystery and miracle of divine love that such a Son should be sent into our world for us! It may well be said, <hi type="italic">So</hi> (wonderfully, so amazingly, so incredibly) <hi type="italic">God loved the world.</hi> 3. That God loved us first, and in the circumstances in which we lay: <hi type="italic">Herein is love</hi> (unusual unprecedented love), <hi type="italic">not that we loved God, but that he loved us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.10">v. 10</reference>. He loved us, when we had no love for him, when we lay in our guilt, misery, and blood, when we were undeserving, ill-deserving, polluted, and unclean, and wanted to be washed from our sins in sacred blood. 4. That he gave us his Son for such service and such an end. (1.) For such service, <hi type="italic">to be the propitiation for our sins;</hi> consequently to die for us, to die under the law and curse of God, to <hi type="italic">bear our sins in his own body,</hi> to be crucified, to be wounded in his soul, and pierced in his side, to be dead and buried for us (<reference osisRef="1John.4.10">v. 10</reference>); and then, (2.) For such an end, for such a good and beneficial end to us—<hi type="italic">that we might live through him</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.9">v. 9</reference>), might live for ever through him, might live in heaven, live with God, and live in eternal glory and blessedness with him and through him: O what love is here! Then, <div eID="gen33735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33736" type="x-p"/> III. Divine love to the brethren should constrain ours: <hi type="italic">Beloved</hi> (I would adjure you by your interest in my love to remember), <hi type="italic">if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.11">v. 11</reference>. This should be an invincible argument. The example of God should press us. <hi type="italic">We should be followers</hi> (or imitators) <hi type="italic">of him, as his dear children.</hi> The objects of the divine love should be the objects of ours. Shall we refuse to love those whom the eternal God hath loved? We should be admirers of his love, and lovers of his love (of the benevolence and complacency that are in him), and consequently lovers of those whom he loves. The general love of God to the world should induce a universal love among mankind. <hi type="italic">That you may be the children of your Father who is in heaven; for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth his rain on the just and on the unjust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Matt. v. 45</reference>. The peculiar love of God to the church and to the saints should be productive of a peculiar love there: <hi type="italic">If God so loved us, we ought</hi> surely (in some measure suitably thereto) <hi type="italic">to love one another.</hi> <div eID="gen33736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33737" type="x-p"/> IV. The Christian love is an assurance of the divine inhabitation: <hi type="italic">If we love one another, God dwelleth in us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">v. 12</reference>. Now God dwelleth in us, not by any visible presence, or immediate appearance to the eye (<hi type="italic">no man hath seen God at any time,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">v. 12</reference>), but by his Spirit (<reference osisRef="1John.4.13">v. 13</reference>); or, "<hi type="italic">No man hath seen God at any time;</hi> he does not here present himself to our eye or to our immediate intuition, and so he does not in this way demand and exact our love; but he demands and expects it in that way in which he has thought meet to deserve and claim it, and that is in the illustration that he has given of himself and of his love (and thereupon of his loveliness too) in the catholic church, and particularly in the brethren, the members of that church. In them, and in his appearance for them and with them, is God to be loved; and thus, <hi type="italic">if we love one another, God dwelleth in us.</hi> The sacred lovers of the brethren are the temples of God; the divine Majesty has a peculiar residence there." <div eID="gen33737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33738" type="x-p"/> V. Herein the divine love attains a considerable end and accomplishment in us: "<hi type="italic">And his love is perfected in us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">v. 12</reference>. It has obtained its completion in and upon us. God's love is not perfected in him, but in and with us. His love could not be designed to be ineffectual and fruitless upon us; when its proper genuine end and issue are attained and produced thereby, it may be said to be perfected; so faith is perfected by its works, and love perfected by its operations. When the divine love has wrought us to the same image, to the love of God, and thereupon to the love of the brethren, the children of God, for his sake, it is therein and so far perfected and completed, though this love of ours is not at present perfect, nor the ultimate end of the divine love to us." How ambitious should we be of this fraternal Christian love, when God reckons his own love to us perfected thereby! To this the apostle, having mentioned the high favour of God's dwelling in us, subjoins the note and character thereof: <hi type="italic">Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.13">v. 13</reference>. Certainly this mutual inhabitation is something more noble and great than we are well acquainted with or can declare. One would think that to speak of God dwelling in us, and we in him, were to use words too high for mortals, had not God gone before us therein. What this indwelling imports has been briefly explained on <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">ch. iii. 24</reference>. What it fully is must be left to the revelation of the blessed world. But this mutual inhabitation we know, says the apostle, <hi type="italic">because he hath given us of his spirit;</hi> he has lodged the image and fruit of his Spirit in our hearts (<reference osisRef="1John.4.13">v. 13</reference>), and <hi type="italic">the Spirit that he hath given us</hi> appears to be his, or of him, since it is <hi type="italic">the Spirit of power,</hi> of zeal and magnanimity for God, <hi type="italic">of love</hi> to God and man, <hi type="italic">and of a sound mind,</hi> of an understanding well instructed in the affairs of God and religion, and his kingdom among men, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2 Tim. i. 7</reference>.
entries.99e9ff6981cee020d51ffb3486ffaf54b6aba2b8: <div eID="gen33738" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33739" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And we have seen and do testify that the Father sent the Son <hi type="italic">to be</hi> the Saviour of the world. <hi type="super">15</hi> Whosoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwelleth in him, and he in God. <hi type="super">16</hi> And we have known and believed the love that God hath to us. God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him. <div eID="gen33739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33740" type="x-p"/> Since faith in Christ works love to God, and love to God must kindle love to the brethren, the apostle here confirms the prime article of the Christian faith as the foundation of such love. Here, <div eID="gen33740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33741" type="x-p"/> I. He proclaims the fundamental article of the Christian religion, which is so representative of the love of God: <hi type="italic">And we have seen, and do testify, that the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.14">v. 14</reference>. We here see, 1. The Lord Jesus's relation to God; he is Son to the Father, such a Son as no one else is, and so as to be God with the Father. 2. His relation and office towards us—<hi type="italic">the Saviour of the world;</hi> he saves us by his death, example, intercession, Spirit, and power against the enemies of our salvation. 3. The ground on which he became so—by the mission of him: <hi type="italic">The Father sent the Son,</hi> he decreed and willed his coming hither, in and with the consent of the Son. 4. The apostle's assurance of this—he and his brethren had seen it; they had seen the Son of God in his human nature, in his holy converse and works, in his transfiguration on the mount, and in his death, resurrection from the dead, and royal ascent to heaven; they had so seen him as to be satisfied that he was the <hi type="italic">only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.</hi> 5. The apostle's attestation of this, in pursuance of such evidence: "<hi type="italic">We have seen and do testify.</hi> The weight of this truth obliges us to testify it; the salvation of the world lies upon it. The evidence of the truth warrants us to testify it; our eyes, and ears, and hands, have been witnesses of it." Thereupon, <div eID="gen33741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33742" type="x-p"/> II. The apostle states the excellency, or the excellent privilege attending the due acknowledgment of this truth: <hi type="italic">Whosoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwelleth in him, and he in God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.15">v. 15</reference>. This confession seems to include faith in the heart as the foundation of it, acknowledgment with the mouth to the glory of God and Christ, and profession in the life and conduct, in opposition to the flatteries or frowns of the world. Thus <hi type="italic">no man says that Jesus is the Lord but by the Holy Ghost,</hi> by the external attestation and internal operation of the Holy Ghost, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. xii. 3</reference>. And so he who thus confesses Christ, and God in him, is enriched with or possessed by the Spirit of God, and has a complacential knowledge of God and much holy enjoyment of him. Then, <div eID="gen33742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33743" type="x-p"/> III. The apostle applies this in order to the excitation of holy love. God's love is thus seen and exerted in Christ Jesus; <hi type="italic">and</hi> thus <hi type="italic">have we known and believed the love that God hath to us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">v. 16</reference>. The Christian revelation is, what should endear it to us, the revelation of the divine love; the articles of our revealed faith are but so many articles relating to the divine love. The history of the Lord Christ is the history of God's love to us; all his transactions in and with his Son were but testifications of his love to us, and means to advance us to the love of God: <hi type="italic">God was in Christ reconciling the world unto himself,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19">2 Cor. v. 19</reference>. Hence we may learn, <div eID="gen33743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33744" type="x-p"/> 1. That <hi type="italic">God is love</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.16">v. 16</reference>); he is essential boundless love; he has incomparable incomprehensible love for us of this world, which he has demonstrated in the mission and mediation of his beloved Son. It is the great objection and prejudice against the Christian revelation that the love of God should be so strange and unaccountable as to give his own eternal Son for us; it is the prejudice of many against the eternity and the deity of the Son that so great a person should be given for us. It is, I confess, mysterious and unsearchable; but there are <hi type="italic">unsearchable riches in Christ.</hi> It is a pity that the vastness of the divine love should be made a prejudice against the revelation and the belief of it. But what will not God do when he designs to demonstrate the height of any perfection of his? When he would show somewhat of his power and wisdom, he makes such a world as this; when he would show more of his grandeur and glory, he makes heaven for the ministering spirits that are before the throne. What will he not do then when he designs to demonstrate his love, and to demonstrate his highest love, or that he himself is love, or that love is one of the most bright, dear, transcendent, operative excellencies of his unbounded nature; and to demonstrate this not only to us, but to the angelic world, and to the principalities and powers above, and this not for our surprise for a while, but for the admiration, and praise, and adoration, and felicity, of our most exalted powers to all eternity? What will not God then do? Surely then it will look more agreeable to the design, and grandeur, and pregnancy of his love (if I may so call it) to give an eternal Son for us, than to make a Son on purpose for our relief. In such a dispensation as that of giving a natural, essential, eternal Son for us and to us, he will commend his love to us indeed; and what will not the God of love do when he designs to commend his love, and to commend it in the view of heaven, and earth, and hell, and when he will commend himself and recommend himself to us, and to our highest conviction, and also affection, as love itself? And what if it should appear at last (which I shall only offer to the consideration of the judicious) that the divine love, and particularly God's love in Christ, should be the foundation of the glories of heaven, in the present enjoyment of those ministering spirits that comported with it, and of the salvation of this world, and of the torments of hell? This last will seem most strange. But what if therein it should appear not only that God is love to himself, in vindicating his own law, and government, and love, and glory, but that the damned ones are made so, or are so punished, (1.) Because they despised the love of God already manifested and exhibited. (2.) Because they refused to be beloved in what was further proposed and promised. (3.) Because they made themselves unmeet to be the objects of divine complacency and delight? If the conscience of the damned should accuse them of these things, and especially of rejecting the highest instance of divine love, and if the far greatest part of the intelligent creation should be everlastingly blessed through the highest instance of the divine love, then may it well be inscribed upon the whole creation of God, <hi type="italic">God is love.</hi> <div eID="gen33744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33745" type="x-p"/> 2. That hereupon <hi type="italic">he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">v. 16</reference>. There is great communion between the God of love and the loving soul; that is, him who loves the creation of God, according to its different relation to God, and reception from him and interest in him. He that dwells in sacred love has <hi type="italic">the love God shed abroad upon his heart,</hi> has the impress of God upon his spirit, the Spirit of God sanctifying and sealing him, lives in the meditation, views, and tastes of the divine love, and will ere long go to dwell with God for ever.
entries.8c59991c08fa8f68ee7585104a4a3534c9e03e9f: <div eID="gen33745" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Love. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 80.)</title> <div sID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world. <hi type="super">18</hi> There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love. <hi type="super">19</hi> We love him, because he first loved us. <hi type="super">20</hi> If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen? <hi type="super">21</hi> And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also. <div eID="gen33746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having thus excited and enforced sacred love from the great pattern and motive of it, the love that is and dwells in God himself, proceeds to recommend it further by other considerations; and he recommends it in both the branches of it, both as love to God, and love to our brother or Christian neighbour. <div eID="gen33747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> I. As love to God, to the <hi type="italic">primum amabile—the first and chief of all amiable beings and objects,</hi> who has the confluence of all beauty, excellence, and loveliness, in himself, and confers on all other beings whatever renders them good and amiable. Love to God seems here to be recommended on these accounts:—1. It will give us peace and satisfaction of spirit in the day when it will be most needed, or when it will be the greatest pleasure and blessing imaginable: <hi type="italic">Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.17">v. 17</reference>. There must be a day of universal judgment. Happy they who shall have holy fiducial boldness before the Judge at that day, who shall be able to lift up their heads, and to look him in the face, as knowing he is their friend and advocate! Happy they who have holy boldness and assurance in the prospect of that day, who look and wait for it, and for the Judge's appearance! So do, and so may do, the lovers of God. Their love to God assures them of God's love to them, and consequently of the friendship of the Son of God; the more we love our friend, especially when we are sure that he knows it, the more we can trust his love. As God is good and loving, and faithful to his promise, so we can easily be persuaded of his love, and the happy fruits of his love, when we can say, <hi type="italic">Thou that knowest all things knowest that we love thee. And hope maketh not ashamed;</hi> our hope, conceived by the consideration of God's love, will not disappoint us, <hi type="italic">because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost that is given to us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.5.5">Rom. v. 5</reference>. Possibly here by the love of God may be meant our <hi type="italic">love to God,</hi> which is <hi type="italic">shed abroad upon our hearts by the Holy Ghost;</hi> this is the foundation of our hope, or of our assurance that our hope will hold good at last. Or, if by the love of God be meant the sense and apprehension of his love to us, yet this must suppose or include us as lovers of him in this case; and indeed the sense and evidence of his love to us do shed abroad upon our hearts love to him; and thereupon we have confidence towards him and peace and joy in him. He will give the crown of righteousness to all that love his appearing. And we have this boldness towards Christ because of our conformity to him: <hi type="italic">Because as he is so are we in this world,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.17">v. 17</reference>. Love hath conformed us to him; as he was the great lover of God and man, he has taught us in our measure to be so too, and he will not deny his own image. Love teaches us to conform in sufferings too; we suffer for him and with him, and therefore cannot but hope and trust that we shall also be glorified together with him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2 Tim. ii. 12</reference>. 2. It prevents or removes the uncomfortable result and fruit of servile fear: <hi type="italic">There is no fear in love</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">v. 18</reference>); so far as love prevails, fear ceases. We must here distinguish, I judge, between fear and being afraid; or, in this case, between the fear of God and being afraid of him. The fear of God is often mentioned and commanded as the substance of religion (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.17">1 Pet. ii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 7</reference>); and so it imports the high regard and veneration we have for God and his authority and government. Such fear is constant with love, yea, with perfect love, as being in the angels themselves. But then there is a being afraid of God, which arises from a sense of guilt, and a view of his vindictive perfections; in the view of them, God is represented as a consuming fire; and so fear here may be rendered <hi type="italic">dread; There is no dread in love.</hi> Love considers its object as good and excellent, and therefore amiable, and worthy to be beloved. Love considers God as most eminently good, and most eminently loving us in Christ, and so puts off dread, and puts on joy in him; and, as love grows, joy grows too; so that <hi type="italic">perfect love casteth out fear</hi> or dread. Those who perfectly love God are, from his nature, and counsel, and covenant, perfectly assured of his love, and consequently are perfectly free from any dismal dreadful suspicions of his punitive power and justice, as armed against them; they well know that God loves them, and they thereupon triumph in his love. That <hi type="italic">perfect love casteth out fear</hi> the apostle thus sensibly argues: that which casteth out torment casteth out fear or dread: <hi type="italic">Because fear hath torment</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">v. 18</reference>)—fear is known to be a disquieting torturing passion, especially such a fear as is the dread of an almighty avenging God; but perfect love casteth out torment, for it teaches the mind a perfect acquiescence and complacency in the beloved, and therefore <hi type="italic">perfect love casteth out fear.</hi> Or, which is here equivalent, <hi type="italic">he that feareth is not made perfect in love</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">v. 18</reference>); it is a sign that our love is far from being perfect, since our doubts, and fears, and dismal apprehensions of God, are so many. Let us long for, and hasten to, the world of perfect love, where our serenity and joy in God will be as perfect as our love! 3. From the source and rise of it, which is the antecedent love of God: <hi type="italic">We love him, because he first loved us,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.19">v. 19</reference>. His love is the incentive, the motive, and moral cause of ours. We cannot but love so good a God, who was first in the act and work of love, who loved us when we were both unloving and unlovely, who loved us at so great a rate, who has been seeking and soliciting our love at the expense of his Son's blood; and has condescended to beseech us to be reconciled unto him. Let heaven and earth stand amazed at such love! His love is the productive cause of ours: <hi type="italic">Of his own will</hi> (of his own free loving will) <hi type="italic">begat he us. To those that love him all things work together for good, to those who are the called according to his purpose.</hi> Those <hi type="italic">that love God are the called</hi> thereto <hi type="italic">according to his purpose</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Rom. viii. 28</reference>); according to whose purpose they are called is sufficiently intimated in the following clauses: <hi type="italic">whom he did predestinate</hi> (or antecedently purpose, to the image of his Son) <hi type="italic">those he also called,</hi> effectually recovered thereto. The divine love stamped love upon our souls; may the Lord still and further direct our hearts into the love of God! <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.5">2 Thess. iii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen33748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33749" type="x-p"/> II. As love to our brother and neighbour in Christ; such love is argued and urged on these accounts:—1. As suitable and consonant to our Christian profession. In the profession of Christianity we profess to love God as the root of religion: "<hi type="italic">If then a man say,</hi> or profess as much as thereby to say, <hi type="italic">I love God,</hi> I am a lover of his name, and house, and worship, <hi type="italic">and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">hate his brother,</hi> whom he should love for God's sake, <hi type="italic">he is a liar</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.4.20">v. 20</reference>), he therein gives his profession the lie." That such a one loves not God the apostle proves by the usual facility of loving what is seen rather than what is unseen: <hi type="italic">For he that loveth not his brother, whom he hath seen, how can he love God, whom he hath not seen?</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.20">v. 20</reference>. The eye is wont to affect the heart; things unseen less catch the mind, and thereby the heart. The incomprehensibleness of God very much arises from his invisibility; the member of Christ has much of God visible in him. How then shall the hater of a visible image of God pretend to love the unseen original, the invisible God himself? 2. As suitable to the express law of God, and the just reason of it: <hi type="italic">And this commandment have we from him, that he who loveth God love his brother also,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.4.21">v. 21</reference>. As God has communicated his image in nature and in grace, so he would have our love to be suitably diffused. We must love God originally and supremely, and others in him, on the account of their derivation and reception from him, and of his interest in them. Now, our Christian brethren having a new nature and excellent privileges derived from God, and God having his interest in them as well as in us, it cannot but be a natural suitable obligation <hi type="italic">that he who loves God should love his brother also.</hi>  <chapter eID="1John.4"/> <div eID="gen33749" type="x-p"/>

entries.8c88707d3e9a42e532f01b6eb5a7fd3df017d188: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18956"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen40810" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1John.4.1-1John.4.21">1Jo 4:1-21</reference>. Tests of False Prophets. Love, the Test of Birth from God, and the Necessary Fruit of Knowing His Great Love in Christ to Us.<div eID="gen40810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18956"/><hi type="bold">1. Beloved--</hi>the affectionate address wherewith he calls their attention, as to an important subject.<div eID="gen40811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every spirit--</hi>which presents itself in the person of a prophet. The Spirit of truth, and the spirit of error, speak by men's spirits as their organs. There is but one Spirit of truth, and one spirit of Antichrist.<div eID="gen40812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">try--</hi>by the tests (<reference osisRef="1John.4.2">1Jo 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.3">3</reference>). All believers are to do so: not merely ecclesiastics. Even an angel's message should be tested by the word of God: much more men's teachings, however holy the teachers may seem.<div eID="gen40813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because, &c.--</hi>the reason why we must "try," or test the spirits.<div eID="gen40814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">many false prophets--</hi>not "prophets" in the sense "foretellers," but organs of the spirit that inspires them, teaching accordingly either truth or error: "many Antichrists."<div eID="gen40815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are gone out--</hi>as if from God.<div eID="gen40816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the world--</hi>said alike of good and bad prophets (2Jo 7). The world is easily seduced (<reference osisRef="1John.4.4">1Jo 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.5">5</reference>). <div eID="gen40817" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab3acd8e8644a9489a4c5d1b8236effed991fc57: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18957"/><div sID="gen40818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18957"/><hi type="bold">2. Hereby--</hi>"Herein."<div eID="gen40818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know ... the Spirit of God--</hi>whether he be, or not, in those teachers professing to be moved by Him.<div eID="gen40819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Every spirit--</hi>that is, Every teacher claiming inspiration by the Holy Spirit.<div eID="gen40820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">confesseth--</hi>The truth is taken for granted as established. Man is required to confess it, that is, in his teaching to profess it openly.<div eID="gen40821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jesus Christ is come in the flesh--</hi>a twofold truth confessed, that Jesus is the Christ, and that He is come (the Greek perfect tense implies not a mere past historical fact, as the aorist would, but also the present continuance of the fact and its blessed effects) in the flesh ("clothed with flesh": not with a mere seeming humanity, as the Docetæ afterwards taught: He therefore was, previously, something far above flesh). His flesh implies His death for us, for only by assuming flesh could He die (for as God He could not), <reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">He 2:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.14">10, 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.16">16</reference>; and His death implies His LOVE for us (<reference osisRef="John.15.13">Joh 15:13</reference>). To deny the reality of His flesh is to deny His love, and so cast away the root which produces all true love on the believer's part (1Jo 4:9-11, 19). Rome, by the doctrine of the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mary, denies Christ's proper humanity. <div eID="gen40822" type="x-p"/>
entries.d27475b2cfc6e7ae67259b0dc30c2ceb0d1aea95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18958"/><div sID="gen40823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18958"/><hi type="bold">3. confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh--</hi>Irenæus [3.8], Lucifer, Origen, on <reference osisRef="Matt.25.14">Mt 25:14</reference>, and Vulgate read, "Every spirit which destroys (sets aside, or does away with) Jesus (Christ)." Cyprian and Polycarp support English Version text. The oldest extant manuscripts, which are, however, centuries after Polycarp, read, "Every spirit that confesseth not (that is, refuses to confess) Jesus" (in His person, and all His offices and divinity), omitting "is come in the flesh."<div eID="gen40823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye have heard--</hi>from your Christian teachers.<div eID="gen40824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">already is it in the world--</hi>in the person of the false prophets (<reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1Jo 4:1</reference>). <div eID="gen40825" type="x-p"/>
entries.56dc50e4c935bdc81c53ce624168fbc20a33fc63: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18959"/><div sID="gen40826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18959"/><hi type="bold">4. Ye--</hi>emphatical: Ye who confess Jesus: in contrast to "them," the false teachers.<div eID="gen40826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40827" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overcome them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1Jo 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.5.5">5</reference>); instead of being "overcome and brought into (spiritual) bondage" by them (<reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>). <reference osisRef="John.10.8">Joh 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.5">5</reference>, "the sheep did not hear them": "a stranger will they not follow, but will flee from him: for they know not the voice of strangers."<div eID="gen40827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that is in you--</hi>God, of whom ye are.<div eID="gen40828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40829" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that is in the word--</hi>the spirit of Antichrist, the devil, "the prince of this world." <div eID="gen40829" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0ea35331ff68756e6c5ea7b60d39ddbf3fd9f8a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18960"/><div sID="gen40830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18960"/><hi type="bold">5. of the world--</hi>They derive their spirit and teaching from the world, "unregenerate human nature, ruled over and possessed by Satan, the prince of this world" [Alford].<div eID="gen40830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak they of the word--</hi>They draw the matter of their conversation from the life, opinions, and feelings of the world.<div eID="gen40831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the world heareth them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.15.18">Joh 15:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.15.19">19</reference>). The world loves its own. <div eID="gen40832" type="x-p"/>
entries.627474aad4dee4ec25faed9cb05e1445258fdcc9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18961"/><div sID="gen40833" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18961"/><hi type="bold">6. We--</hi>true teachers of Christ: in contrast to them.<div eID="gen40833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40834" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">are of God--</hi>and therefore speak of God: in contrast to "speak they of the world," <reference osisRef="1John.4.5">1Jo 4:5</reference>.<div eID="gen40834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40835" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth God--</hi>as his Father, being a child "of God" (<reference osisRef="1John.2.13">1Jo 2:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen40835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40836" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heareth us--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="John.18.37">Joh 18:37</reference>, "Every one that is of the truth, heareth My voice."<div eID="gen40836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40837" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hereby--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1John.4.2-1John.4.6">1Jo 4:2-6</reference>); by their confessing, or not confessing, Jesus; by the kind of reception given them respectively by those who know God, and by those who are of the world and not of God.<div eID="gen40837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40838" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit of truth--</hi>the Spirit which comes from God and teaches truth.<div eID="gen40838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40839" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spirit of error--</hi>the spirit which comes from Satan and seduces into error. <div eID="gen40839" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a7b7a640e4abec3fb285e9ffab75bee64cbab9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18962"/><div sID="gen40840" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18962"/>7. Resumption of the main theme (<reference osisRef="1John.2.29">1Jo 2:29</reference>). Love, the sum of righteousness, is the test of our being born of God. Love flows from a sense of God's love to us: compare <reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1Jo 3:16</reference>, which <reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference> resumes; and <reference osisRef="1John.4.13">1Jo 4:13</reference> with <reference osisRef="1John.3.24">1Jo 3:24</reference>, which similarly <reference osisRef="1John.4.13">1Jo 4:13</reference> resumes. At the same time, <reference osisRef="1John.4.7-1John.4.21">1Jo 4:7-21</reference> is connected with the immediately preceding context, <reference osisRef="1John.4.2">1Jo 4:2</reference> setting forth Christ's incarnation, the great proof of God's love (<reference osisRef="1John.4.10">1Jo 4:10</reference>).<div eID="gen40840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40841" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beloved--</hi>an address appropriate to his subject, "love."<div eID="gen40841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40842" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">love--</hi>All love is from God as its fountain: especially that embodiment of love, God manifest in the flesh. The Father also is love (<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>). The Holy Ghost sheds love as its first fruit abroad in the heart.<div eID="gen40842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40843" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knoweth God--</hi>spiritually, experimentally, and habitually. <div eID="gen40843" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1a61e80856b807d49e62c3296d1376217883e0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18963"/><div sID="gen40844" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18963"/><hi type="bold">8. knoweth not--</hi>Greek aorist: not only knoweth not now, but never knew, has not once for all known God.<div eID="gen40844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40845" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God is love--</hi>There is no Greek article to love, but to God; therefore we cannot translate, Love is God. God is fundamentally and essentially LOVE: not merely is loving, for then John's argument would not stand; for the conclusion from the premises then would be this, This man is not loving: God is loving; therefore he knoweth not God IN SO FAR AS God is loving; still he might know Him in His other attributes. But when we take love as God's essence, the argument is sound: This man doth not love, and therefore knows not love: God is essentially love, therefore he knows not God. <div eID="gen40845" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9e9fdd3a56709e4f31c8aa8c1fbb405fe72af6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18964"/><div sID="gen40846" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18964"/><hi type="bold">9. toward us--</hi>Greek, "in our case."<div eID="gen40846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40847" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent--</hi>Greek, "hath sent."<div eID="gen40847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40848" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the world--</hi>a proof against Socinians, that the Son existed before He was "sent into the world." Otherwise, too, He could not have been our life (<reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference>), our "propitiation" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.10">1Jo 4:10</reference>), or our "Saviour" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.14">1Jo 4:14</reference>). It is the grand proof of God's love, His having sent "His only-begotten Son, that we might live through Him," who is the Life, and who has redeemed our forfeited life; and it is also the grand motive to our mutual love. <div eID="gen40848" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8a9650ca5404c1358f16e0da78a79b3163a9335: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18965"/><div sID="gen40849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18965"/><hi type="bold">10. Herein is love--</hi>love in the abstract: love, in its highest ideal, is herein. The love was all on God's side, none on ours.<div eID="gen40849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not that we loved God--</hi>though so altogether worthy of love.<div eID="gen40850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40851" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he loved us--</hi>though so altogether unworthy of love. The Greek aorist expresses, Not that we did any act of love at any time to God, but that He did the act of love to us in sending Christ. <div eID="gen40851" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae772511cec2370c034c517179b07eed4ff1f933: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18966"/><div sID="gen40852" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18966"/>11. God's love to us is the grand motive for our love to one another (<reference osisRef="1John.3.16">1Jo 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen40852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if--</hi>as we all admit as a fact.<div eID="gen40853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40854" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we ... also--</hi>as being born of God, and therefore resembling our Father who is love. In proportion as we appreciate God's love to us, we love Him and also the brethren, the children (by regeneration) of the same God, the representatives of the unseen God. <div eID="gen40854" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f9f06ddc3f83b4adb14f91663a3cef5931324b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18967"/><div sID="gen40855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18967"/>12. God, whom no man hath seen at any time, hath appointed His children as the visible recipients of our outward kindness which flows from love to Himself, "whom not having seen, we love," compare Notes, <reference osisRef="1John.4.11">1Jo 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.19">1Jo 4:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.20">20</reference>. Thus <reference osisRef="1John.4.12">1Jo 4:12</reference> explains why, instead (in <reference osisRef="1John.4.11">1Jo 4:11</reference>) of saying, "If God so loved us, we ought also to love God," he said, "We ought also to love one another."<div eID="gen40855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If we love one another, God dwelleth in us--</hi>for God is love; and it must have been from Him dwelling in us that we drew the real love we bear to the brethren (<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.4.16">16</reference>). John discusses this in <reference osisRef="1John.4.13-1John.4.16">1Jo 4:13-16</reference>.<div eID="gen40856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40857" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his love--</hi>rather, "the love of Him," that is, "to Him" (<reference osisRef="1John.2.5">1Jo 2:5</reference>), evinced by our love to His representatives, our brethren.<div eID="gen40857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40858" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is perfected in us--</hi>John discusses this in <reference osisRef="1John.4.17-1John.4.19">1Jo 4:17-19</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="1John.2.5">1Jo 2:5</reference>, "is perfected," that is, attains its proper maturity. <div eID="gen40858" type="x-p"/>
entries.c971830ac9ca700abc6ee1b2ce21414e03f95f89: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18968"/><div sID="gen40859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18968"/><hi type="bold">13. Hereby--</hi>"Herein." The token vouchsafed to us of God's dwelling (Greek, "abide") in us, though we see Him not, is this, that He hath given us "of His Spirit" (<reference osisRef="1John.3.24">1Jo 3:24</reference>). Where the Spirit of God is, there God is. One Spirit dwells in the Church: each believer receives a measure "of" that Spirit in the proportion God thinks fit. Love is His first-fruit (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>). In Jesus alone the Spirit dwelt without measure (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>). <div eID="gen40859" type="x-p"/>
entries.72395a690f8b87a9eee4f713266b1c0256a43734: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18969"/><div sID="gen40860" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18969"/><hi type="bold">14. And we--</hi>primarily, we apostles, Christ's appointed eye-witnesses to testify to the facts concerning Him. The internal evidence of the indwelling Spirit (<reference osisRef="1John.4.13">1Jo 4:13</reference>) is corroborated by the external evidence of the eye-witnesses to the fact of the Father having "sent His Son to be the Saviour of the world."<div eID="gen40860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seen--</hi>Greek, "contemplated," "attentively beheld" (see on <reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1Jo 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen40861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sent--</hi>Greek, "hath sent": not an entirely past fact (aorist), but one of which the effects continue (perfect tense). <div eID="gen40862" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9a2b83417e37996146795b1e6d4adfeb761712d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18970"/><div sID="gen40863" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18970"/><hi type="bold">15. shall confess--</hi>once for all: so the Greek aorist means.<div eID="gen40863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40864" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that Jesus is the Son of God--</hi>and therefore "the Saviour of the world" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.14">1Jo 4:14</reference>). <div eID="gen40864" type="x-p"/>
entries.26027c82be37e2f0a961ac2f12d86d250d498856: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18971"/><div sID="gen40865" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18971"/><hi type="bold">16. And we--</hi>John and his readers (not as <reference osisRef="1John.4.14">1Jo 4:14</reference>, the apostles only).<div eID="gen40865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">known and believed--</hi>True faith, according to John, is a faith of knowledge and experience: true knowledge is a knowledge of faith [Luecke].<div eID="gen40866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40867" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to us--</hi>Greek, "in our case" (see on <reference osisRef="1John.4.9">1Jo 4:9</reference>).<div eID="gen40867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40868" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dwelleth--</hi>Greek, "abideth." Compare with this verse, <reference osisRef="1John.4.7">1Jo 4:7</reference>. <div eID="gen40868" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b20df46b0ef8f45b49d956f7d318e43e1855f08: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18972"/><div sID="gen40869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18972"/>17-18. (Compare <reference osisRef="1John.3.19-1John.3.21">1Jo 3:19-21</reference>.)<div eID="gen40869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40870" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our love--</hi>rather as the Greek, "LOVE (in the abstract, the principle of love [Alford]) is made perfect (in its relations) with us." Love dwelling in us advances to its consummation "with us" that is, as it is concerned with us: so Greek. <reference osisRef="Luke.1.58">Lu 1:58</reference>, "showed mercy upon (literally, 'with') her": 2Jo 2, the truth "shall be with us for ever."<div eID="gen40870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boldness--</hi>"confidence": the same Greek as <reference osisRef="1John.3.21">1Jo 3:21</reference>, to which this passage is parallel. The opposite of "fear," <reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>. Herein is our love perfected, namely, in God dwelling in us, and our dwelling in God (<reference osisRef="1John.4.16">1Jo 4:16</reference>), involving as its result "that we can have confidence (or boldness) in the day of judgment" (so terrible to all other men, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">Ac 24:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.16">Ro 2:16</reference>).<div eID="gen40871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because, &c.--</hi>The ground of our "confidence" is, "because even as He (Christ) is, we also are in this world" (and He will not, in that day, condemn those who are like Himself), that is, we are righteous as He is righteous, especially in respect to that which is the sum of righteousness, love (<reference osisRef="1John.3.14">1Jo 3:14</reference>). Christ IS righteous, and love itself, in heaven: so are we, His members, who are still "in this world." Our oneness with Him even now in His exalted position above (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>), so that all that belongs to Him of righteousness, &c., belongs to us also by perfect imputation and progressive impartation, is the ground of our love being perfected so that we can have confidence in the day of judgment. We are in, not of, this world. <div eID="gen40872" type="x-p"/>
entries.3a7964f6d7445dd8f4ec379d05d4ab1f55a4356a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18974"/><div sID="gen40876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18974"/><hi type="bold">19. him--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. Translate, We (emphatical: WE on our part) love (in general: love alike Him, and the brethren, and our fellow men), because He (emphatical: answering to "we"; because it was He who) first loved us in sending His Son (Greek aorist of a definite act at a point of time). He was the first to love us: this thought ought to create in us love casting out fear (<reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>). <div eID="gen40876" type="x-p"/>
entries.c892b01db95fe8652fe384ddd3f1b2586ea6a037: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18975"/><div sID="gen40877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18975"/><hi type="bold">20. loveth not ... brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen--</hi>It is easier for us, influenced as we are here by sense, to direct love towards one within the range of our senses than towards One unseen, appreciable only by faith. "Nature is prior to grace; and we by nature love things seen, before we love things unseen" [Estius]. The eyes are our leaders in love. "Seeing is an incentive to love" [OECUMENIUS]. If we do not love the brethren, the visible representatives of God, how can we love God, the invisible One, whose children they are? The true ideal of man, lost in Adam, is realized in Christ, in whom God is revealed as He is, and man as he ought to be. Thus, by faith in Christ, we learn to love both the true God, and the true man, and so to love the brethren as bearing His image.<div eID="gen40877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath seen--</hi>and continually sees. <div eID="gen40878" type="x-p"/>
entries.625ef63f01f27c05ab6b7a48e97bf5dccebb0b5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18976"/><div sID="gen40879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18976"/>21. Besides the argument (<reference osisRef="1John.4.20">1Jo 4:20</reference>) from the common feeling of men, he here adds a stronger one from God's express commandment (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.39">Mt 22:39</reference>). He who loves, will do what the object of his love wishes.<div eID="gen40879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he who loveth God--</hi>he who wishes to be regarded by God as loving Him. <chapter eID="1John.4"/>

entries.b0f91079d1c19e11912fc04a02f9e3a2d49f63ba: <div eID="gen55194" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen55195" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55196" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55196" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen55195" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen55197" type="x-p"/> We must not believe every teacher who professes to have a Divine commission to preach, but try such, whether they be of God; and the more so because many false prophets are gone out into the world, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.1">1Jn 4:1</reference>. Those who deny that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh have the spirit of antichrist, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.2">1Jn 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.3">1Jn 4:3</reference>. The followers of God have been enabled to discern and overcome them, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.4-1Jn.4.6">1Jn 4:4-6</reference>. The necessity of love to God and one another shown, from God's love to us, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.7-1Jn.4.11">1Jn 4:7-11</reference>. Though no man hath seen God, yet every genuine Christian knows him by the spirit which God has given him, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.12">1Jn 4:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.13">1Jn 4:13</reference>. The apostles testified that God sent his Son to be the Savior of the world; and God dwelt in those who confessed this truth, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.14">1Jn 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.15">1Jn 4:15</reference>. God is love, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.16">1Jn 4:16</reference>. The nature and properties of perfect love, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.17">1Jn 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.18">1Jn 4:18</reference>. We love him because he first loved us, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.19">1Jn 4:19</reference>. The wickedness of pretending to love God while we hate one another, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.20">1Jn 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.21">1Jn 4:21</reference>. <div eID="gen55197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen55198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55199" type="x-p"/> Beloved, believe not every spirit - Do not be forward to believe every teacher to be a man sent of God. As in those early times every teacher professed to be inspired by the Spirit of God, because all the prophets had come thus accredited, the term spirit was used to express the man who pretended to be and teach under the Spirit's influence. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.1-1Cor.12.12">1Cor 12:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Tim 4:1</reference>. <div eID="gen55199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55200" type="x-p"/> Try the Spirits - Δοκιμαζετε τα πνευματα· Put these teachers to the proof. Try them by that testimony which is known to have come from the Spirit of God, the word of revelation already given. <div eID="gen55200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55201" type="x-p"/> Many false prophets - Teachers not inspired by the Spirit of God, are gone out into the world - among the Jewish people particularly, and among them who are carnal and have not the Spirit.
entries.32779f564a8f3f68e82c460da7a2c05b2841a5f7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen55201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55202" type="x-p"/> Hereby know ye the Spirit of God - We know that the man who teaches that Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah, and that he is come in the flesh, is of God - is inspired by the Divine Spirit; for no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost.
entries.8d5d4c8bfe67959694b310381e580d513c872236: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen55202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55203" type="x-p"/> Every spirit - Every teacher, that confesseth not Jesus, is not of God - has not been inspired by God. The words εν σαρκι εληλυθοτα, is come in the flesh, are wanting in AB, several others, both the Syriac, the Polyglot Arabic, Ethiopic, Coptic, Armenian, and Vulgate; in Origen, Cyril, Theodoret, Irenaeus, and others. Griesbach has left them out of the text. <div eID="gen55203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55204" type="x-p"/> Spirit of antichrist - All the opponents of Christ's incarnation, and consequently of his passion, death, and resurrection, and the benefits to be derived from them. <div eID="gen55204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55205" type="x-p"/> Ye have heard that it should come - See <reference osisRef="2Thes.2.7">2Thes 2:7</reference>. <div eID="gen55205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55206" type="x-p"/> Even now already is it in the world - Is working powerfully both among the Jews and Gentiles.
entries.92df0d2d4ccf0a80df75406ff51dc718ce1ac75b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen55206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55207" type="x-p"/> Ye are of God - Ye are under the influence of the Divine Spirit, and have overcome them - your testimony, proceeding from the Spirit of Christ, has invalidated theirs which has proceeded from the influence of Satan; for greater is the Holy Spirit which is in you, than the spirit which is in the world.
entries.7c6c582c6116c74a260994f832a521dc29ed7faa: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen55207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55208" type="x-p"/> We are of God - We, apostles, have the Spirit of God, and speak and teach by that Spirit. He that knoweth God - who has a truly spiritual discernment, heareth us - acknowledges that our doctrine is from God; that it is spiritual, and leads from earth to heaven. <div eID="gen55208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55209" type="x-p"/> Hereby know we the Spirit of truth - The doctrine and teacher most prized and followed by worldly men, and by the gay, giddy, and garish multitude, are not from God; they savor of the flesh, lay on no restraints, prescribe no cross-bearing, and leave every one in full possession of his heart's lusts and easily besetting sins. And by this, false doctrine and false teachers are easily discerned.
entries.1ed241c8478a897b1f643bcf639543b91e7318b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen55209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55210" type="x-p"/> Beloved, let us love one another - And ever be ready to promote each other's welfare, both spiritual and temporal. <div eID="gen55210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55211" type="x-p"/> For love is of God - And ever acts like him; he loves man, and daily loads him with his benefits. He that loveth most has most of God in him; and he that loveth God and his neighbor, as before described and commanded, is born of God, εκ του Θεου γεγεννηται, is begotten of God - is a true child of his heavenly Father, for he is made a partaker of the Divine nature; and this his love to God and man proves.
entries.8728f51d6d2bd8def99f8544b579a6e6c3df2d89: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen55211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55212" type="x-p"/> He that loveth not - As already described, knoweth not God - has no experimental knowledge of him. <div eID="gen55212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55213" type="x-p"/> God is love - An infinite fountain of benevolence and beneficence to every human being. He hates no thing that he has made. He cannot hate, because he is love. He causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends his rain on the just and the unjust. He has made no human being for perdition, nor ever rendered it impossible, by any necessitating decree, for any fallen soul to find mercy. He has given the fullest proof of his love to the whole human race by the incarnation of his Son, who tasted death for every man. How can a decree of absolute, unconditional reprobation, of the greater part or any part of the human race, stand in the presence of such a text as this? It has been well observed that, although God is holy, just, righteous, etc., he is never called holiness, justice, etc., in the abstract, as he is here called Love. This seems to be the essence of the Divine nature, and all other attributes to be only modifications of this.
entries.d8b548c0887fa0bb9d00869ed31fbc0f134a4488: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen55213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55214" type="x-p"/> In this was manifested the love of God - The mission of Jesus Christ was the fullest proof that God could give, or that man could receive, of his infinite love to the world. <div eID="gen55214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55215" type="x-p"/> That we might live through him - The whole world was sentenced to death because of sin; and every individual was dead in trespasses and sins; and Jesus came to die in the stead of the world, and to quicken every believer, that all might live to him who died for them and rose again. This is another strong allusion to <reference osisRef="Joh.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference> : God so loved the world, that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life; where the reader is requested to see the note on <reference osisRef="Joh.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>.
entries.2178a7ea463420003477f0483e5f38f984d6b63c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen55215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55216" type="x-p"/> Not that we loved God - And that he was thereby induced to give his Son to be a propitiation for our sins. No: we were enemies to God, and yet Christ died for our ungodly souls. (See <reference osisRef="Rom.5.6-Rom.5.11">Rom 5:6-11</reference>, and the notes there.) So it was God's love, not our merit, that induced him to devise means that his banished might not be expelled from him.
entries.6d1d95d703f349d3d06e0d695da90e031b24e323: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen55216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55217" type="x-p"/> If God so loved us - Without any reason or consideration on our part, and without any desert in us; we ought also, in like manner, to love one another, and not suspend our love to a fellow-creature, either on his moral worth or his love to us. We should love one another for God's sake; and then, no unkind carriage of a brother would induce us to withdraw our love from him; for if it have God for its motive and model, it will never fail.
entries.94a63b3162bfb331470e681df8653ec16beaef32: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen55217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55218" type="x-p"/> No man hath seen God at any time - The very words, with the change of ἑωρακε for τεθεαται, of this apostle in his gospel, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>. We may feel him, though we cannot see him; and if we love one another he dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us - it has then its full accomplishment, having moulded us according to its own nature.
entries.adf29aeb54b572c3f777ebdfa79a61121c769e62: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen55218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55219" type="x-p"/> Hereby know we, etc. - See the note on <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.24">1Jn 3:24</reference>.
entries.bbc01cc96db7bf227beb5f5ca5fff5e6a1e3e265: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen55219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55220" type="x-p"/> And we have seen - Jesus Christ manifested in the flesh; see <reference osisRef="1Jn.1.1">1Jn 1:1</reference>, etc.; and do testify - bear witness, in consequence of having the fullest conviction, that the Father sent the son to be the Savior of the world. We have had the fullest proof of this from his doctrine and miracles, which we heard and saw during the whole time that he sojourned among men.
entries.f8ed19d84d72704a3b324b98edd76a8a5d6d2a56: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen55220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55221" type="x-p"/> Whosoever shall confess - Much stress is laid on this confession, because the false teachers denied the reality of the incarnation; but this confession implied also such a belief in Christ as put them in possession of his pardoning mercy and indwelling Spirit.
entries.a936564e695089def34c8cb845fe05debf711865: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen55221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen55222" type="x-p"/> God is love - See on <reference osisRef="1Jn.4.8">1Jn 4:8</reference> (note).
